COMMENTS OF PUBLIC INTEREST ORGANIZATIONS 
 
  
Pursuant to Rule 211 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (FERC or 
Commission) Rules of Practice and Procedure,1 Appalachian Voices, Clean Air Task Force, 
Earthjustice, the Environmental Defense Fund, PennFuture, and the Sierra Club, together Public 
Interest Organizations (PIOs), respectfully submit these comments to respond to PJM 
Interconnection, L.L.C.’s (PJM) answer2 to the Commission’s February 20, 2025 Order 
Instituting Proceeding Under Section 206 of the Federal Power Act and Consolidating with Other 
Proceedings (Show Cause Order).3   
I. 
Introduction 
By 2029, PJM’s load growth forecast is expected to top 24.8 GW,4 which is a stark 
contrast from the flat demand growth that most regions have experienced over the last decade.5  
Most of the demand increase is attributable to data centers that process Artificial Intelligence 
(AI), cloud services and search algorithms.  Total energy consumption in the United States from

(“PJM Answer”). 
3 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Order Instituting Proceeding Under Section 206 of the Federal Power Act and 
Consolidating with Other Proceedings, Docket Nos. EL25-49-000, et al. (“Show Cause Order”).

5 
 
data centers is expected to grow from  4.4 percent of total energy consumption to between 6.7 to 
12 percent by 2028.6  Since the Commission supports providing regulatory “certainty and 
clarity” to data centers seeking to interconnect to the grid,7 and the lead time to construct data 
centers is shorter than the average time to interconnect new generators and build traditional 
transmission infrastructure,8 a variety of stakeholders, including data center owners and 
independent power producers (IPP), are interested in pursuing more co-location arrangements to 
power those facilities. 
One example is Constellation and its complaint against PJM arguing that PJM should 
revise its tariff to allow co-location arrangements that do not require load to acquire network 
transmission service.  Relatedly, Constellation is also pursuing approval to merge with Calpine, a 
transaction that, if approved, would give Constellation leverage to use its existing nuclear 
generation fleet to co-locate with large loads, according to parties who protested the merger 
application.9  The IPPs will make decisions regarding co-location based on their profit motive, 
without accounting for the interests of other ratepayers in reliability and appropriate cost-
allocation.  Recent improvements to PJM’s ability to interconnect supply obviate the need for 
these arrangements.  
  RMI’s 2024 study of PJM’s supply projections concluded that even with 10 GW of 
anticipated generator retirements, PJM is on track to meet or exceed supply needs for 2030 load 
forecasts.10  RMI’s analysis estimates that between 5.2GW and 6.85 GW of new supply will

come from interconnection projects in PJM’s “Fast Lane” process.11  And on April 18, 2025, 
PJM announced that its Fast Lane interconnection process cleared for construction 
approximately 19 GW of new supply.  In addition, implementing Grid Enhancing Technologies 
(GETs) within the next few years, an approach that the Commission champions in its Order 2023 
rule on interconnection reforms,12 could enable PJM to interconnect up to 6.3 GW of new supply 
once it fully embraces the form and intention of the rule.13 
Consistent with the need to address these developments, the Commission’s Show Cause 
Order seeks input on whether PJM’s existing tariff provisions and related agreements governing 
co-location arrangements are just, reasonable, and not unduly discriminatory or preferential.  
While options 1-2 are favorable since they require that load acquire network service, the status 
quo provisions are not sustainable in the face of a huge influx of these arrangements and need for 
substantial changes to the study processes, large load forecast process, and cost allocation.14  
As discussed below, these options are unjust and unreasonable since they are based on load 
forecasts that lack adequate vetting mechanisms to remove speculative requests and could enable 
co-location arrangements that unlawfully shift resulting network upgrade costs to customers that 
do not receive benefits that are roughly commensurate with the estimated upgrade costs.   
Inaccurate load forecasts have more definitive consequences for ratepayers: overstating PJM’s 
regional needs for multi-billion-dollar transmission assets and the reserve margin for its capacity 
market.

12 Improvements to Generator Interconnection Procedures and Agreements, 184 FERC ¶ 61,054 (2023) (“Order No. 
2023”) 
13 RMI, GETting Interconnected in PJM (Feb. 2024) at 5-7, https://rmi.org/insight/analyzing-gets-as-a-tool-for-
increasing-interconnection-throughput-from-pjms-queue/.

Since co-location arrangements provide limited, if any, system-wide benefits, the 
Commission should not authorize the new arrangements that PJM offers in its response (options 
4-8), without substantial safeguards to prevent unlawful cost shifting, reliability shortfalls, 
among other issues.  Options 4 and 5, which allow existing resources to enter into dedicated, co-
location arrangements, could unnecessarily increase PJM’s required reserve margins and could 
require reliability upgrades.  And option 6, which could enable expedited interconnection of 
generation resources dedicated to large loads, could further exacerbate backlogs in the 
interconnection queue and, therefore, threaten reliability. Additionally, such expedited 
interconnection may violate the anti-discrimination provisions of the Federal Power Act. Even 
allowing a co-location generator to take non-firm service has consequences if the data center’s 
business model requires it to run 24/7 (options 7-8) since it will rely on back-up diesel 
generators, which are both harmful to communities and pose reliability risks. In sum, for PJM to 
meet the moment, it must take measures beyond relying on co-location arrangements. The large 
scale and quick pace of load growth in PJM’s projections requires PJM to instead focus on 
implementing a robust forecasting process to guard against speculation, and fully comply with 
FERC’s rules on transmission planning, generator interconnection, and cost allocation processes 
to ensure that large load customers that will come online can integrate into the grid without 
imposing unjust, unreasonable, and unduly discriminatory or preferential rates, terms, and 
conditions on non-large-load customers.     
II. 
PJM’s OATT, the Amended and Restated Operating Agreement of PJM, and the 
Reliability Assurance Agreement Among Load Serving Entities in PJM’s Region are 
Unjust, Unreasonable, and Unduly Discriminatory and Preferential. 
At the outset, we reiterate that PJM has a number of tools at its disposal to ensure that 
new entry can rise to the challenge of new load growth.  Nevertheless, as it pertains specifically

8 
 
to co-location arrangements between generation and large load customers, we identify two 
primary issues with PJM’s existing Tariff and current practices.  First, PJM’s use of the 
Necessary Study Process, Supplemental Projects, and Regional Transmission Expansion 
Planning (“RTEP”) Process allocate the costs of transmission upgrades in an unjust and 
unreasonable manner.  Second, PJM’s load forecasting practices under Practice Manual 19 fail to 
ensure accuracy and protect against speculative or duplicative estimates. 
A. PJM’s Existing Study Processes to Identify and Allocate Costs for 
Transmission Upgrades is Unjust and Unreasonable. 
For co-location arrangement Options 1 and 2, PJM’s current practices assess the 
transmission upgrades associated with co-location agreements through a combination of three 
processes: the Necessary Study, Transmission Owner Load Integration Studies, and RTEP.15  
Though these studies do result in the co-location arrangement paying for some portion of the 
identified upgrades, they fail to ensure that the co-location arrangement pays its fair share of 
these upgrade costs under cost allocation principles.  We note that the cost of transmission 
upgrades related to interconnection-like processes are distinct from broader transmission rates.  
Under PJM’s existing co-location options, co-located load is treated as Network Load and thus 
does pay for transmission service.16  As explained in greater detail in Section III (A), we believe 
it is appropriate for co-located load to pay for transmission service, and thus support PJM’s 
treatment of co-located load as Network Load.17  This section focuses solely on the cost-
allocation for transmission system upgrades caused by the shift to a co-location agreement, not 
the costs of ongoing delivery of services via the transmission system following the initial shift. 
 
15 See PJM Answer at 47. 
16 PJM Answer at 9-12 (tables of existing options, noting that under each option, load takes NITS service). 
17 See infra at 24.

9 
 
1. The Necessary Study Process for Co-Location Arrangements is 
Opaque and Not Suited for Co-Location, Causing Unjust and 
Unreasonable Rates.  
As the Commission finds in the Show Cause Order, inadequate interconnection service 
provisions for co-location arrangements, “especially regarding studies of the impacts of those 
arrangements,” may render PJM’s Tariff unjust and unreasonable.18  We agree that the Necessary 
Study “may not be fully capturing the transmission system impacts of co-locating load,” and thus 
could result in co-location arrangements with already-operational generators “not paying the 
costs of network upgrades that would be caused by the co-location.”19  As Suzanne Glatz and 
Abraham Silverman explained in the Commission’s technical conference docket, while from an 
engineering perspective there is little difference between co-location and other load 
interconnections with generation behind the meter, from a regulatory and cost allocation 
perspective, they are treated differently—resulting in “similar electrical impacts, but vastly 
different rate impacts.”20 
The Necessary Study Process was designed for studying potential impacts from more 
minor, routine changes to the electrical characteristics of existing generating units previously 
studied by PJM,21 and is a poor fit for the more significant nature of an existing generator 
entering into a co-location arrangement for all or most of its energy production.  As Glatz and 
Silverman’s comments explain, in the standard usage of the Necessary Study Process for routine 
maintenance type updates, PJM grants no new grid services or rights.22  For example, the 
Commission has accepted Necessary Study Agreements that enable generators to replace wind

19 Id. 
20 Post-Technical Conference Comments of Suzanne Glatz and Abraham Silverman, Docket No. AD24-11-000 at 1 
(Dec. 9, 2024), Accession No. 20241209-5149.

22 Comments of Glatz and Silverman at 5.

software.25  In contrast, however, PJM has not allowed the addition of battery storage to existing 
generation to go through the Necessary Study Process, in large part because batteries can act as 
load.26  PJM offers no explanation for why co-located load is thus offered preferential treatment.  
Moreover, unlike the sorts of routine changes to update and maintain the function of a generator 
described above, co-location arrangements both make more significant electrical changes and 
effectively grant the existing generator a new right to serve load directly.  Finally, it’s worth 
noting that the costs of upgrades that PJM identifies are allocated to the existing generator, rather 
than the load. This reflects the nature of the Necessary Study Process as originally intended—
focused on changes to existing generators. 
PJM’s main defense of the narrowness of the Necessary Study Process for studying co-
location with an existing generator is that other study processes are also used.27  However, each 
of the other studies that PJM identifies pass costs to broader sections of load—not the large load 
customer(s) causing the need for the upgrades. These studies include the Transmission Owner 
(TO) load integration study, which identifies needed local transmission upgrades that will be 
proposed to the PJM Transmission Expansion Advisory Committee (TEAC) as Supplemental 
Projects; the PJM do no harm study, which identifies any broader transmission impacts caused 
by the proposed Supplemental Project, which will need to be addressed by an expansion of the 
Supplemental Project; and the RTEP Process, which identifies any regional transmission

upgrades caused by an aggregate of load additions pass costs to broader sections of load.  The 
unjust and unreasonable nature of this treatment will be detailed in the next section, but at base: 
the Necessary Study Process is the only process that PJM uses to identify the direct 
interconnection-related cost responsibility of co-locating large load with an existing generator, 
and it fails to do so with appropriate accuracy. 
Moreover, the Necessary Study Process occurs entirely behind closed doors.  The 
Commission should independently find the opaqueness of this process to be unjust and 
unreasonable.  Under the Necessary Study Process, there is no transparency regarding what 
specific changes to an existing generator that PJM is studying (e.g., what the timeline for the 
load addition may be, or even how much load addition is requested), and no disclosure of the 
results of the study.  The public can only access this type of information much later in the study 
process, when PJM files a revised Interconnection Service Agreement for the existing generator 
at FERC.  As the Organization of PJM States pointed out in their comments to the technical 
conference, this is a much different level of transparency than in other circumstances in which 
generator capacity is removed from the system—e.g., retirement.28  
2. PJM’s Reliance on Transmission Owner Load Integration 
Studies and Regional Transmission Expansion Planning to 
Identify Upgrades to Resolve Transmission Needs Associated 
with Co-Located Load Results in Unjust and Unreasonable 
Rates. 
 
As PJM explains, the Necessary Study Process, which identifies generator-level upgrades 
for existing generators, is followed by a TO Load Integration Study to identify upgrades to 
resolve any local transmission reliability needs that arise as a result of the co-location 
 
28 Post Technical Conference Comments of the Organization of PJM States, Inc., Docket No. AD24-11-000 at 3-4 
(Dec. 9, 2024), Accession No. 20241209-5086.

12 
 
arrangement, and then the RTEP process to identify upgrade needs arising from the aggregation 
of co-location arrangements.29  Yet when the TO Load Integration Study identifies so-called 
Supplemental Projects to resolve the needs, the costs of which are allocated not just to the large 
load customer that triggered the local transmission reliability need, but to the TO’s entire local 
utility footprint in that zone.  And despite this cost allocation, there is no guarantee that these 
projects provide greater system benefits.  Thus, this process’s failure to allocate a proportional 
amount of these costs specifically to large load customers is a straightforward violation of cost 
causation, and an unjust and unreasonable rate.    
We note that the transmission upgrades required to reliably integrate co-location 
agreements are differently situated from transmission upgrades required to reliably deactivate 
uneconomic generation (the costs of which are also socialized to load) and thus should be treated 
differently.  Specifically, co-located load will continue to be the beneficiary of a functional grid 
going forward—and indeed the principal beneficiary of transmission upgrades specifically 
triggered by the co-location arrangements—whereas a retiring generator will not derive benefit 
from the grid in the future.  Thus, while only the remaining load—not the deactivating 
generator—would utilize the transmission upgrades associated with retirements, co-located load 
will continue to rely on, and benefit greatly from, such upgrades. 
 
There is no guarantee that Supplemental Projects, nor projects selected through RTEP, 
provide any system benefits, beyond the circular reasoning that such projects will prevent 
reliability issues associated with co-location.  As demonstrated in the chart below, many early 
examples of transmission upgrades driven by data center loads have not led to system benefits,

Moreover, building out the transmission system in response to discrete, emergent needs 
rather than through proactive, forward-looking, system-wide planning fails to identify the most 
cost-effective future transmission portfolio, which would solve the reliability issues associated 
with co-location agreements and provide broader system benefits.30  The magnitude of estimated

to identify, evaluate, and select more efficient or cost-effective transmission solutions to address Long-Term

solutions that are relatively inefficient or less cost-effective because they address only short-term transmission

load growth necessitates a more systematic approach to addressing these needs to ensure 
reliability and affordability for all transmission system users.  Transmission system upgrades are 
needed and the cost of some upgrades driven by load growth are appropriately shared by load 
across the region. But the band-aid approach of Supplemental Projects triggered by each new 
large load customer is going to cost all ratepayers more. 
We recognize that under PJM’s existing options (Options 1 and 2), co-located load is 
treated as Network Load and thus pays for Network Integration Transmission Service (NITS), 
including the costs of Supplemental Projects folded into NITS rates.31  However, this treatment 
still puts regular residential consumers on the hook for Supplemental Projects they did not 
cause—and from which they often do not meaningfully benefit—in violation of the cost 
causation principle.  Under PJM’s existing Tariff, there is high risk that co-located load 
underpays for the upgrades it triggers by only taking sole responsibility for costs arising in the 
Necessary Study Process (to the extent an existing generator passes the costs on to the co-located 
load, that is).  Moreover, this potential cost-dodging is especially concerning given that some 
commenters argue that co-located load should not be charged for transmission service.32 
Finally, like the Necessary Study Process, the TO Load Integration Study and the 
Supplemental Projects Process that it triggers are opaque and lack critical regulatory oversight.  
As the Commission has previously noted, “the planning for Supplemental Projects is done almost 
entirely by the PJM Transmission Owners, with PJM playing a relatively minor role in which it

cost allocation reforms will benefit customers by leading to more efficient or cost-effective transmission investment, 
thereby helping to ensure just and reasonable rates”).

reliability impacts.”33  This lack of oversight and transparency is particularly concerning since 
Supplemental Projects make up the majority of transmission spending in PJM and are a leading 
cause of cost increases in the region.34  The lack of ready access to information around the TO 
Load Integration Study and resulting Supplemental Projects perpetuates a paradigm in which 
ratepayer advocates cannot effectively challenge the prudency of transmission investments and 
cost allocation at either the federal or the state level.  At a time when affordability of electricity is 
paramount, the Commission should not bless the continuation of this approach to co-location 
arrangements. 
B. The Load Forecasting Provisions in PJM’s Practice Manual 19 Lack 
Controls and Standards to Ensure Accuracy and Protect Against 
Speculative Forecast Estimates. 
PJM’s Tariff is unjust and unreasonable because it lacks sufficient controls and standards 
to ensure large load forecast accuracy and to protect against speculative large load forecast 
estimates.  PJM’s large load forecasting process does not substantively account for speculative 
load additions, thus rendering the process and resulting forecast, as well as everything that relies 
on that forecast, unjust and unreasonable.  In addition, PJM’s Tariff is unjust and unreasonable

the filed tariff, contrary to the long-standing “rule of reason” (Rule of Reason Doctrine).35  
In the Show Cause Order, the Commission asked whether PJM should “consider changes 
to load forecasting methods, informational postings, or the reserve margin study process to better 
plan for and address the resource adequacy and reliability impacts of co-location 
arrangements.”36  PJM itself identified that there is a need to “clarify or enhance existing 
planning processes,” including “addressing risks that arise based on the existing load forecasting 
process,” for which PJM has requested “Commission guidance.”37  Below we argue that: (1) 
PJM’s existing large load forecasting process is deficient; (2) the process should be included in 
the Tariff consistent with the Commission’s Rule of Reason Doctrine; and (3) the Commission 
should direct PJM to revise its load forecasting process to improve its accuracy. 
1. PJM’s Load Forecast Process Fails to Provide Standard, 
Comparable Parameters and Processes to Accurately Forecast 
Large Loads. 
PJM’s load forecasting process, described in its Manual 19, does not include sufficient 
controls or standards to prevent speculative additions of large load from entering PJM’s load 
forecast, which can cause significant costs and result in unjust and unreasonable rates.  PJM’s 
load forecasting procedure can largely be found on three pages in PJM Manual 19, attachment 
B.38   Also, PJM relies on each load serving entity or electric distribution company (LSE/EDC) 
to develop its own internal forecasting criteria, which unsurprisingly leads to widely differing

C. PJM Must Not Limit States’ Authority Over the Co-Located Generation 
Mix. 
The Commission also correctly notes that under the FPA,124 states retain authority over 
the “mix” (that is, the portfolio characteristics) of a state’s generating fleet, as well as the 
locations and permission to operate for specific generating facilities.125  While generator 
interconnections to the transmission system are a matter of Commission jurisdiction, and the 
Commission through its FPA Section 215 authority may approve reliability standards for 
generators, the Commission has no role to directly dictate, subsidize, discourage, or ban 
particular generating projects or types of generating projects.  With these jurisdictional contours 
in mind, any FERC-jurisdictional tariff structure that may facilitate co-location arrangements 
must be neutral to technology type and not favor or disfavor any type of co-located generator, 
lest it encroach on a state’s desire to structure co-location arrangements according to a preferred 
mix, consistent with state authority under the FPA.

V. 
Conclusion 
Given the scale and pace of data center load growth in PJM’s projections and, therefore, 
the high likelihood that generators and large loads will increasingly seek to implement co-
location arrangements, the Commission should take action to ensure that PJM revises its existing 
tariff and related agreements for co-location arrangements (Options 1 and 2), consistent with our 
comments, to ensure that rates, terms, and conditions for Commission-jurisdictional services are 
just, reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential.   We agree that large loads should 
remain ineligible for the behind-the-meter option (Option 3).  And, while we see limited to no 
utility with requiring PJM to implement new co-location arrangements (Options 4-8), if the 
Commission disagrees, we request that it require PJM to implement the provisions that mitigate 
the risks that we discuss above (e.g., unlawful cost shifts).
